summary: A 1970 note commenting on the protocol described in RFC 36. It updates RFC 36 with feedback from the RAND authors. It is one of the discussion contributions in the early protocol design process.

eli5.summary: More feedback on a proposed set of rules for how computers talk, sent from people at another lab.

questions: what was the err command in the early arpanet protocol
what is the ncp in the arpanet
subtitle: RAND's suggested additions to the early host-to-host protocol: errors, queries, termination and broadcast.

tldr.problem: The early host-to-host protocol described in RFC 36 had no built-in way to report errors, check connection status or tear down all of a program's connections at once.
tldr.mechanism: The authors propose new control commands (error, query, program termination, host status) and two data prefixes (transmit and broadcast), and they also voice concern about the protocol's complexity.
tldr.outcome: These are suggestions for inclusion in the April 28th protocol specifications, not a finished design, and the authors say they have not studied the connection-setup problem in depth.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 39 as updating RFC 36, with no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a set of 1970 suggestions to a draft protocol, and the text does not say which were adopted.

sections.title: Suggestions for the April 28th Protocol
sections.content:
RAND authors E. Harslem and J. Heafner offer suggestions to be considered as additions to the April 28th 1970 protocol grammar specifications. The protocol is the one described in RFC 36, and this note updates it.

The additions are small new commands, written in angle brackets in the style of the grammar: <ERR>, <QRY>, <TER>, <HCU>, <HGD>, <TRN> and <BDC>. The note ends with a criticism of the request-for-connection structure.
sections.eli5: Some people read a draft rulebook and wrote back with a list of extra rules they would like to add, plus a worry that part of it is too complicated.

sections.title: Error Messages and Queries
sections.content:
The <ERR> <Code> <Command in error> message is meant as a debugging aid for checking out Network Control Programs. There are three classes of error: content errors, status errors, and resource allocation or exhaustion. The code names the class and the offending member of it, and the bad command is returned to the sending NCP for analysis.

Examples given include messages sent over blocked links (status), closing an unconnected link (content), and connection table overflow (resource). Resource errors should be followed by a <CLS> in response to the <RFC>, the protocol's own connection-request command.

Queries extend this with limited error recovery, avoiding re-initialization of an NCP. <QRY> <My Socket> asks the remote NCP for the status of all connections to the user given in My Socket. The reply form <QRY> <Your Socket> <Text> carries the status in its text. To ask about all connections to a remote HOST, My Socket is zero.
sections.eli5: If a computer sends a message that does not make sense, the other one hands it back with a note saying what kind of mistake it was. A computer can also ask, what is going on with our connections.

sections.title: Termination, Host Status and Broadcast
sections.content:
<TER> <My Socket> supplements <CLS>. It severs all communication between a program and the programs in a given HOST that it is connected to, doing what would otherwise take multiple <CLS> commands. My Socket holds the sender's user number.

The pair <HCU> (HOST coming up) and <HGD> (HOST voluntarily going down) suit asynchronous, interrupt-driven programs, as opposed to the more conventional post and poll method.

<TRN> <Body> and <BDC> <Body> are not sent over the control link but over links assigned to user programs. The prefix tells the receiving NCP what to do with the body: <TRN> passes it to a single process, while <BDC> distributes it over all receiving connections linked to the sender. For a broadcast request, the NCP generates one <BDC> to each HOST the sender is connected to.
sections.eli5: There would be one command to hang up on everyone at once, a message that says, I am turning on, or I am shutting down, and a way to send one note to one friend or to a whole group.

sections.title: Concerns About Connection Setup
sections.content:
The authors criticize the request-for-connection (RFC) and dynamic reconnection scheme. They say it is complex, proliferates control messages, causes queues to be artificially imposed by the protocol (remote AEN assignment), and ignores the case where only controlling process A knows that slave process B should be rung out in a dynamic reconnection.

The criticism is not meant to hold up changes to the RFC structure by April 28th, nor to reflect on those who planned it. The authors say they have not studied the problem. They raise concern about complexity and response times, say it deserves more study after the current specifications have been exercised, and hope to offer constructive suggestions later.
sections.eli5: They also say, nicely, that one part of the draft seems to need too many steps and may be slow. They promise to help find something simpler once people have tried it.

references.text: The protocol whose April 28th grammar specifications these suggestions would extend.
